Sunder

SUN-der · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To sunder is to split apart or rend.

A single act of betrayal was enough to sunder an alliance that had lasted for generations.

Worked Example

The earthquake sundered the old highway into two pieces, leaving a gap too wide for cars to cross.

Sunder describes a forceful, often dramatic splitting apart of something that was once whole, whether a physical object, a relationship, or a political alliance.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

sever: To sever is to cut something off cleanly and completely -- a rope, a wire, formal ties -- and it works at any scale, even the smallest. To sunder is grander and more violent: a dramatic tearing apart of something large that was once whole, like an alliance or a nation.

rupture: A rupture is a sudden bursting or breaking open, usually of something under pressure -- a pipe, a tank, a blood vessel. To sunder is a wider, more dramatic splitting: the whole thing is torn into separate pieces, not burst open at a single point.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

unite: bring together as one

merge: combine into a single whole

Where it sits · how violent and final the break — separate → sunder → shatter

separate vs. sunder: To separate two things can be gentle and reversible -- unstacking chairs, sorting laundry -- far milder than to sunder them, which is a violent, final tearing apart of something once whole.

shatter vs. sunder: To shatter something breaks it into countless irreparable pieces, an even more violent split than sundering it.

Put it together

Put it together: syndrian ("to separate") = to split apart.

Use the root in a new word: sundry

Use the root in a new word: sundry: The same Old English root gives us "sundry," meaning various or separate, as in "sundry items" -- things that are all different from one another.

Word Choice

Sunder is a dramatic, almost literary word for forceful separation -- it fits a shattered alliance or a broken nation far better than an everyday, minor disagreement.
